newsitem.title: USA: Clinton budget seeks $18 billion in welfare fix.
newsitem.headline: Clinton budget seeks $18 billion in welfare fix.

text.p: President Clinton will ask Congress for about $18 billion over five years to aid legal immigrants and Food Stamps recipients who will lose benefits under a new welfare law, congressional sources said Tuesday.

Clinton's fiscal 1998 budget plan, to be sent to Congress Thursday, asks Congress to change the welfare law so legal immigrants who become disabled after entering the United States will be eligible for federal disability and Medicaid health benefits, according to budget documents.
Under the welfare law, hundreds of thousands of legal immigrants will lose Food Stamps, Supplemental Security Income disability aid and other assistance by late August.

The National Governors' Association Tuesday ended a contentious four-day meeting by passing a resolution that calls on Congress to aid immigrants who will lose benefits -- without reopening the welfare bill.

Under pressure from congressional Republicans, the governors backed off their original proposal specifically stating that elderly and disabled immigrants who were in the United States before the law took effect should remain eligible for Food Stamps and disability aid.
A Republican staff aide predicted major resistance to the administration plan.
The Clinton budget proposal will ensure that more than 250,000 legal immigrants who became disabled after entering the United States would continue to receive disability and Medicaid.
It would also continue aid to low income immigrant children, especially the disabled.

The plan does not call on Congress to restore Food Stamps to legal immigrants, but would delay the ban on such aid until the end of September to give immigrants more time to become naturalized citizens.
Under the welfare law, states must begin notifying immigrants this spring that they could lose benefits by August at the latest.

Clinton's budget also tries to restore a provision wiped out in the welfare bill allowing families with high rent and heating bills to deduct a greater proportion of those expenses from their income when applying for Food Stamps.

Putting the so-called excess shelter deduction in place will enable many families to receive higher Food Stamps benefits. Clinton is also proposing to change a provision of the law that allows able-bodied individuals without dependents to receive Food Stamps for only three months in a three year period, unless they are working.
In addition, Clinton is proposing a $3.4 billion package of tax incentives to move welfare recipients to work.
